analysis.one_liner: Caps shipping rates to Hawaii, Alaska, and U.S. territories at international-index levels plus 10%
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a committee or floor vote when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Goods shipped by sea to Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. territories move only on U.S.-flag carriers, a small set of companies protected by federal law from foreign competition, and their rates are high. The bill would have written a definition of a 'reasonable' rate into federal law: a rate would count as reasonable only if it stayed within 10% of a comparable international shipping rate index recognized by the Federal Maritime Commission. It was referred to committee and a subcommittee and never received a markup, committee vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and businesses of Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, Guam, and other noncontiguous areas, who pay inflated ocean freight rates on nearly everything they import, consume, or ship out; lower shipping costs flow through to grocery, energy, and goods prices in places with no cheaper alternative.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the shipping code so a rate in noncontiguous domestic ocean trade is 'reasonable' only if it is within 10 percent of a rate set by a comparable international ocean rate index recognized by the Federal Maritime Commission.

Under current law, rates in this trade are required to be reasonable, but there is no defined benchmark, so carriers' rate filings largely go unchallenged; the bill supplies a concrete standard for the first time.

Because nearly all consumer goods reaching these markets travel on a small number of protected U.S.-flag carriers, a rate benchmark tied to international levels would directly target one of the largest cost-of-living inputs for island and remote communities.

analysis.who_pays: The small group of U.S.-flag ocean carriers that hold the noncontiguous domestic trade (the Jones Act routes), whose rates would be capped near international levels, cutting into margins built on a market closed to foreign competition.

drawbacks.text: International rate indexes reflect ships built and crewed abroad at far lower cost; U.S.-flag carriers in this trade must use U.S.-built, U.S.-crewed vessels, so capping rates within 10% of an international index could make the service uneconomic and risk reduced or less reliable sailings to Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the territories.
The bill names no specific index and leaves the Federal Maritime Commission to 'recognize' a comparable international index, creating questions about how the benchmark would be chosen and enforced.

Rate regulation, even with a defined benchmark, does not address the underlying driver of high rates — the Jones Act restriction itself that bars foreign carriers from these routes — so it treats the symptom rather than the cause.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete for millions of people who pay some of the highest shipping-inflated prices in the country and have no alternative carrier. The main cost is a real design risk: an index tied to foreign-cost shipping could squeeze carriers whose costs are legally higher, and the bill offers no safeguard for service continuity if a carrier cut routes. A more carefully built version would phase in the benchmark or pair it with service obligations.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation subcommittee, and never received a markup or any vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Case (D-HI) introduced the bill on April 13, 2023, joined by Rep. James Moylan.
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation.
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a committee markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill drew one cosponsor, a Republican, alongside its Democratic sponsor, giving it small bipartisan sponsorship but almost no visible support in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The U.S.-flag carriers in the noncontiguous trade are better off, because their rates remain without a defined benchmark and the market stays closed to foreign competition; residents of Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the territories gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: U.S.-flag shipping carriers, at residents' expense

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Democratic sponsor from Hawaii and a Republican cosponsor from Guam — but with only two members behind it, no party took a measurable position and no vote ever recorded the split.

industries.industry: U.S.-flag domestic ocean carriers (Jones Act noncontiguous trade)
industries.note: A handful of carriers hold the legally protected routes between the mainland and Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the territories, and set rates without a defined benchmark. The bill would have capped rates near international levels, reducing revenue those carriers earn from markets where consumers have no alternative.

An international rate index recognized by the Federal Maritime Commission would borrow foreign-market pricing, though the carriers themselves would still be barred from carrying the cargo. The bill's benchmark indirectly legitimizes international rates as the standard of fairness.
